questions.prompt: Why put the rate limiter in the API gateway rather than in each backend service?

options.text: One implementation and rule set, and excess requests are rejected before they reach any backend

questions.explanation: Centralizing the limiter avoids duplicated logic and inconsistent rules, and it shields backends from load they would otherwise have to absorb.

questions.prompt: Each of 50 gateways keeps its own local counter and allows 100 requests per second per key. What's the worst case for one key?

options.text: About 5,000 requests per second, if its traffic spreads across all gateways

questions.explanation: Independent counters each allow the full limit: 50 × 100. A shared counter store, or dividing the limit by the number of gateways, fixes this.

questions.prompt: Two gateways read a counter of 99 (limit 100) at the same moment, both allow the request and both write 100. What fixes this?

options.text: An atomic check-and-spend operation inside the counter store, such as a server-side script

questions.explanation: Read-then-write from separate clients loses updates. Doing the whole check and update as one atomic operation in the store makes concurrent requests see each other's effect.

questions.prompt: Why put the API key in a hash tag such as rl:{key_123}:search-burst?

options.text: So all of a key's counters land on the same shard, letting one atomic call check every rule in a single round trip
Redis requires braces in key names

questions.explanation: A cluster hashes only the part in braces, so related keys share a shard. Atomic multi-key operations only work within one shard.

questions.prompt: The counter store becomes unreachable. Which behaviours are sensible?

options.text: Fail open on normal endpoints, with a local per-gateway fallback limit
Fail closed on login and password-reset endpoints
Reject every request until the store recovers
Alert, and track how long fallback mode is active

questions.explanation: A limiter outage shouldn't become an API outage, so most rules fail open with an approximate local limit. Abuse-sensitive endpoints fail closed. Rejecting everything turns a partial failure into a total one.
